title: ToddyCat
summary: ToddyCat is a tracked threat group that public reporting describes as conducting espionage against government, military, and telecommunications organisations, mainly in Asia and Europe. Vendor reporting describes initial access through internet-facing mail servers, followed by the deployment of several separate backdoor families rather than a single toolkit, which means removing one implant rarely ends the intrusion. Analysts note heavy use of legitimate administration utilities for tunnelling, credential access, and collection, keeping activity close to normal systems management. Evidence tends to appear in web server and mail service logs, in unusual child processes of server services, and in scheduled tasks or services the organisation never provisioned. Because the group is tracked mainly through vendor telemetry, public reporting on its sponsor and on the exact boundaries of the cluster should be treated as provisional and likely to be revised.

beginner.definition: ToddyCat is a name that security companies use for a group of attackers. Public reports say the group targets governments, armies, and telephone companies. It often gets in through mail servers that face the internet. Once inside, it uses several different tools to keep access.
beginner.whyItMatters: Mail servers sit in a special place in your network. They talk to the whole internet, so attackers like them. If such a server is not updated, an intruder can read mail and then move deeper. ToddyCat shows that one break-in can lead to many hidden tools. Knowing the pattern helps you watch your mail servers much more closely.
howItWorks: The group looks for mail servers that are reachable from the internet and still missing security updates.
When it finds one, it uses a flaw in the server software to run its own commands.
It then places several small programs, called backdoors, on the server for later use.
These backdoors let the attackers return even after the first flaw is repaired.
The group also uses normal administration tools, so its actions look like routine work.
It copies documents and email data out slowly, to avoid starting any loud alarms.
beginner.example: Picture a shared mailroom in a big company. The mailroom door opens to the street, because letters must come in from outside. A stranger walks in with a clipboard and starts sorting post. Nobody stops him, because he looks like a temporary worker. Later, he hides spare keys in several drawers. Even when the front door lock is changed, he can still walk in through the drawers he prepared. The staff only notice when they count the keys and find ones they never made.
takeaways: Keep internet-facing mail servers updated, because attackers watch them closely.
Make a list of every tool that runs on your servers, so extra tools stand out.
Read your server logs for odd programs started by mail services.

objectives: Explain what ToddyCat is and which sectors public reporting describes it targeting.
Describe how a compromised internet-facing mail server becomes a foothold for deeper access.
Explain why several independent backdoors change the way an incident is contained.
Recognise the evidence that server and endpoint logs leave around legitimate administration tools.
Assess how provisional vendor attribution affects the way you write a threat assessment.
